previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 55-year-old woman was admitted for recurrent nausea and vomiting, with a history of chronic gastroparesis, recent paraduodenal hernia repair, and multiple prior hospitalizations for similar symptoms. She presented with inability to tolerate oral intake, generalized abdominal pain with vomiting, and new-onset worsening back pain. Initial evaluation revealed leukocytosis, hypokalemia, and a non-obstructive bowel pattern. Imaging identified a new compression fracture in two mid-thoracic vertebrae. A post-pyloric Dobhoff tube was placed and enteral feeding initiated, which she tolerated well for two days before self-removing the tube and expressing readiness for discharge. Her nausea resolved, electrolytes normalized, and pain was controlled with medications. She was discharged home with improved symptoms, new prescriptions for antiemetics, potassium supplementation, and naproxen for back pain, and instructions to follow up with her gastroenterologist and primary care provider regarding long-term feeding options and osteoporosis management.

Of note, this is her fourth admission since ___. Most

presentation. During that admission, her outpatient 
gastroenterologist and surgery consult team were consulted. Her 
outpatient GI (Dr. ___ has been recommending a J 
tube, and the surgery team recommended first more conservative 
therapy with tube feeds via a post-pyloric Dobhoff. She 
tolerated the tube feeds with minimal nausea and vomiting. 
Shortly afterwards however, she removed her dobhoff and stated 
that she was ready to go home. The plan was to continue 
discussions for a long term plan as an outpatient. 

Since discharge, she reports that she has continued to feel 
poorly. Specifically, she reports poor appetite, poor PO intake, 
intermittent nausea, and vomiting. In the 24 hours prior to 
admission, she then developed increased nause, vomiting, and 
abdominal pain. She describes her abdominal pain as the 
following: character is pressure-like, onset was within the last 
24 hours, location is in her diffuse abdomen, and it has been 
gradually getting worse until going to the ED. She received pain 
medications in the ED, and upon arrival to the floor she denies 
any abdominal pain or nausea. 

She feels increasingly frustrated with her frequent admissions 
and feels like she is ""not bouncing back"" like she used to. When 
asked for her goals for this admission, she states that she 
would like a J tube placed. Although she has been hesitant for J 
tube placement in the past, she now feels that it is her only 
chance to improve her strength, nutrition, and well-being. She 
spoke with a friend who has a G tube, who was able to decrease 
many of her fears about a J tube.

Upon arrival in the ED, temp 99.6, HR 149/124 / HR 110, RR 18, 
and pulse ox 98% on room air. Exam was notable for being 
ill-appearing, diffuse tenderness to palpation, and tachycardia 
(HR 110). She received zofran 4mg IV x 2, morphine 4mg IV x 3, 
reglan 10mg IV x 1, and potassium (unclear if she received 40 or 
80 mEq).

radiology_notes.text:
PA AND LATERAL CHEST ___.

HISTORY:  Nausea, vomiting and epigastric pain.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  A scar is again noted laterally in the left mid lung.  No
superimposed consolidation or edema is evident.  There is mild aortic
tortuosity, similar to the prior exam.  The cardiac silhouette is within
normal limits for size and also stable.  No effusion or pneumothorax is noted.
Numerous clips project within the left axilla and there is asymmetry of the
breast shadow suggestive of likely prior lumpectomy and/or radiation of the
left breast.  Numerous surgical apparatus identified at the gastroesophageal
junction similar to the prior exam.  The osseous structures are unremarkable. 
The patient has undergone prior cholecystectomy.

IMPRESSION:
Stable chest x-ray examination.  No acute pulmonary process.  Apparent prior
breast surgery presumably due to breast cancer.  Correlate clinically.
